title: Four evaluation plans
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four People Ops teams are switching on an AI assistant in their HR service desk. All four wrote an evaluation plan first, which already puts them ahead of most.

**One of them is measuring activity and calling it change.** Find it.

artifacts.label: Plan A
artifacts.body: "Before enablement we're saving four numbers from the ticket system: weekly volume, median time to resolution and time to first response separately, the repeat-contact rate, and the top five categories by count — each with the saved query and the population definition. Our change metric is repeat-contact rate on the categories the assistant handles, because a wrong answer produces a second contact. We're tagging AI-involved contacts and repeat contacts from the day before go-live. Kill condition: if repeat-contact rate on tagged categories exceeds 15% for two consecutive weeks, Priya turns it off — she's rehearsed the rollback in sandbox, it takes about twenty minutes. Checked every Friday, decision point at 60 days."

artifacts.label: Plan B
artifacts.body: "We're tracking adoption weekly — unique users, sessions per user, questions answered, and containment rate — with a target of 60% containment by day 90. We'll also run a pulse survey at 30 and 90 days asking employees how satisfied they are with the new assistant and whether they'd recommend it. Deflected tickets times average handling cost gives us the savings figure for the business case. If adoption stalls below 40% we'll run a comms push and manager enablement to drive usage."

artifacts.label: Plan C
artifacts.body: "We baselined volume, cycle time and repeat rate two weeks before launch, with the queries saved. Change metric is time to first response for the leave-and-benefits categories. We're scoping it deliberately narrow — carryover-balance questions only, one business unit, 400 people — because we want a result we can actually read, and we'd rather widen it later than launch broad and learn nothing. Kill condition: Marcus checks at day 45 and pulls it if answer accuracy against the current policy document falls below 95% on a weekly sample of 20. Nobody has performed the rollback yet; it's scheduled for the week before go-live."

artifacts.label: Plan D
artifacts.body: "Baseline is the last twelve months of ticket volume and cost per contact from our annual reporting pack. Change metric is cost per contact, which we expect to fall. We're also logging every answer the assistant gives to a review queue, and a coordinator spot-checks twenty a week against policy. Kill condition: if the assistant produces an answer that creates a compliance issue, we escalate to the HRIS steering group, who can suspend it at any point — that's written into the enablement approval."

reasoning:
**B is activity dressed as change, and it is the most common plan in this market.** Every number in it moves when people use the thing. Unique users, sessions, questions answered, containment — all activity. The pulse survey looks like an experience metric and is not: it asks people how satisfied they are *with the assistant*, which is a question about the tool rather than about whether their problem got solved. IBM's 2018 mandate is the case: usage went to near-universal and HR satisfaction fell from +19 to −35, and every metric on B's list would have improved that year.

The tell is the last sentence. **"If adoption stalls below 40% we'll run a comms push to drive usage"** — the plan has exactly one failure mode and its remedy is more adoption. There is no result B could produce that would mean *this did not help*, which makes it unfalsifiable in the same way Lesson 4's broad pilot is. And the savings figure — deflections times handling cost — counts an abandoned conversation and a confidently wrong answer identically to a genuine fix.

**A is the reference answer.** Four baseline numbers with saved queries and stated populations, a change metric chosen because it *detects a wrong answer* rather than because it looks good, rework tagging in place before go-live, and a kill condition with all four parts — computable threshold, weekly date, named person, and a rollback that has actually been performed with the time recorded.

**C is strong and is the deliberate hard distractor.** The scoping is exemplary — carryover balances only, one unit, 400 people — which is Lesson 4's rule applied properly: narrow until it works rather than broad until it fails. Accuracy against the current policy document is a genuine change metric. Its gaps are honest and small: no rework tagging, so relocated work onto managers and coordinators stays invisible, and **the rollback hasn't been performed yet** — scheduled, which is better than most, and still a hope until somebody does it. If you picked C, you were marking it down for incompleteness rather than for the category error, and the distinction between those two is the exercise.

**D is the interesting failure, because everything in it is real work.** A review queue with weekly spot-checks against policy is a genuine quality control and better than most teams manage. Two things sink it. The baseline is **twelve months of annual-pack reporting**, which cannot be re-run against a stated population and will be argued about rather than compared — Lesson 1's point about saving the query. And cost per contact is a metric that improves if employees give up: **someone who got a wrong answer and stopped asking makes the number better.** Then the kill condition names a committee and a trigger with no threshold, which is escalation rather than a condition — it cannot fire while a sponsor still wants the project, which is Lesson 5's test.

The transferable question: **for each metric, would it still move if the deployment made things worse for employees?** B's would all move upward. D's flagship metric would improve. A's and C's would not.
